title: The STRONG Method
hook: Six index cards on a ferry bench decide whether the megawatts can wait.
counterintuition: STRONG is not a menu of clever moves but a pressure sequence. Each beat earns the next one before the room is asked to decide.
tryThisNow: Map your current pitch as six one-line beats from frame to decision. Mark the beat you usually rush or skip.
keyTakeaway: Use STRONG as an operating sequence: each move earns the next, so the room is guided from first attention to concrete decision without losing control.

breakdown.fastRead:
Petra has six colored index cards on a ferry terminal bench. One says megawatts. One says lease vote. One says decision. The wind project is strong, but the port authority will not hear turbines correctly if the room first sees political risk.

She moves the frame card to the front and the decision card to the end.

That is the point of STRONG. It is a strategic order: set the frame, tell the story, reveal intrigue, offer the prize, nail the hookpoint, and get a decision. A pitch with the right pieces in the wrong order still loses force.
breakdown.deepRead:
Thomas sells naming rights for a minor-league baseball park. His old opening starts with attendance numbers because they are strong. The regional bank hears logo inventory, not community status.

Before the next meeting, he crosses out the attendance-first order. The community-story card moves before the premium-access card, and the branch-opening date moves before the final ask. The same material now has a spine.

STRONG turns the early diagnosis into a method. First, set and own the frame so the room knows what kind of decision it is making. Then tell the story so the facts have a sequence. Then reveal intrigue so attention stays active. Then offer the prize so value does not look needy. Then nail the hookpoint so consequence and desire concentrate. Then get a decision while the room is still warm enough to act.

The order teaches the room what to feel next.

Skip one move and another move has to do impossible work. A hookpoint before story sounds like a slogan. A decision before prize feels like pressure. Intrigue without frame can look like confusion. The method does not replace judgment; it keeps judgment from scattering under live pressure.

Petra does not need a more impressive turbine card. She needs the card to appear after the port has accepted the right frame. If output leads, the lease vote becomes an engineering comparison. If frame leads, output becomes evidence for a public-capacity decision that can move to story, intrigue, prize, hookpoint, and finally the vote.
breakdown.fullRead:
A pilot agenda sits on Rebecca's desk with two coffee rings and red checkmarks. The remote-triage rollout failed with emergency physicians because she jumped from story to decision. She had explained patient-flow stakes, then asked for pilot approval before the room felt curiosity about the new workflow. The objection log tells the truth: software first, suspicion second, no intrigue in between.

The STRONG method exists to prevent that kind of collapse. It gives a live pitch a route. Frame protects the meaning of the room. Story gives the room a sequence it can follow. Intrigue keeps the mind active. Prize protects value and fit. Hookpoint concentrates the peak. Decision turns energy into commitment.

Does every room need the same length for every move? No. A ten-minute investor pitch and a three-minute internal ask have different pacing. The sequence is not a script. It is a set of handoffs. You can compress a handoff, but if you skip it entirely, the next move often lands before the room is ready.

Consider Marc, who owns a fire-damaged inn and wants a construction loan. The charred porch baluster is powerful, but if he opens with grief, the lender may hear sentiment. He lays the loan term sheet, occupancy graph, and charred baluster in sequence. The rebound story has to come before the hookpoint. The hookpoint has to come before terms. The terms have to come before a clean decision. The same objects can either ramble or compel depending on order.

Julia leads an ocean-cleanup robotics team into a marina commission meeting. The sealed robot case is beside a bucket of tangled fishing line. Engineers want to open the case first. Julia shuts it instead. She starts with who owns the marina's reputation after holiday trash weekends, then tells the debris-cost story, then lets curiosity build around the pilot. Only later does the robot appear as a selective answer, not a gadget looking for applause.

That is what an operating sequence does. It stops your favorite proof from rushing the room. It stops your ask from arriving lonely. It lets the material breathe in the order a listener can actually receive.

The named sequence matters because a pitch is easy to scramble under pressure. Someone interrupts. A number gets challenged. A senior person asks for the price early. Without a route, you chase the latest signal. With a route, you can return to the next move instead of dumping every fact at once.

The sequence is not there to make you mechanical. It is there to keep the room from becoming mechanical with you.

A sequence also tells you what to cut. When Sofia moves the terms sheet to the end, she is not hiding terms. She is refusing to let the room price a patent before it understands category, risk, desire, and fit. Under time pressure, the method does not ask for six equal speeches. It asks for six clean handoffs, each short enough to preserve the next one.

examples.title: Petra Moves the Megawatt Card Back

planSpec.domain: offshore wind developer preparing a port-authority lease pitch
planSpec.audience: a project lead with engineering, finance, and political risk all competing for airtime
planSpec.stakes: the lease vote stalls if the pitch opens with turbines before control of the room is set
planSpec.requiredBeat: she rearranges six index cards on the ferry terminal bench until frame comes before megawatt output and decision comes last

examples.scenario: Petra studies six colored index cards on a ferry terminal bench, weighted by a token beside the lease vote date. The megawatt output card is first because the engineering is impressive. She looks at the port agenda and must decide whether to open with turbines or move the frame card ahead of output and leave decision last. The moved card changes the meeting from a feature tour into a public-capacity argument with a vote waiting at the end.
examples.whatToDo: Reorder the cards so frame leads, story follows, intrigue and prize build value, the hookpoint peaks, and the lease decision comes last.
examples.whyItMatters: The port authority will judge the same megawatts differently depending on the frame. Sequence protects the technical proof from arriving before the room can use it.

examples.title: Thomas Crosses Out Attendance First

planSpec.domain: minor-league baseball sponsorship director selling a naming package to a regional bank
planSpec.audience: a sponsorship director who usually starts with attendance numbers
planSpec.stakes: the bank treats the offer as logo inventory unless the sequence builds status and desire first
planSpec.requiredBeat: he crosses out the old attendance-first order and places the community-story card before the premium-access card

examples.scenario: Thomas sits in the minor-league stadium office after the branch-opening call, with a seating chart folded beside sponsor lanyards. His old order starts with attendance numbers, and the bank keeps hearing logo inventory. He crosses that order out, places the community-story card before premium access, and must decide whether attendance supports the story instead of leading it. The seating chart now supports a community story instead of forcing Thomas to sell logo inventory too soon.
examples.whatToDo: Let the bank hear community status before inventory. Put attendance in the story, not at the front, so premium access can feel like a prize.
examples.whyItMatters: Numbers alone make the package comparable. Sequenced after story and status, the same numbers support a stronger reason to want the naming package.

examples.title: Rebecca Finds the Missing Intrigue

planSpec.domain: telemedicine compliance lead pitching a remote-triage rollout to emergency physicians
planSpec.audience: a clinician-administrator who must win a room that distrusts workflow tools
planSpec.stakes: the rollout dies if physicians hear software before status and patient-flow stakes
planSpec.requiredBeat: after a failed pilot meeting, she labels where she skipped intrigue and jumped from story straight to decision

examples.scenario: Rebecca studies a printed pilot agenda at 3:40 p.m. in the hospital admin suite, with two coffee rings and red checkmarks on the page. The patient-flow metric is circled, but the physician objection log is worse. In the postmortem, she labels the skipped handoff: story went straight to pilot approval before intrigue made the workflow desirable. The skipped handoff shows why approval sounded premature before the doctors had a reason to want the pilot.
examples.whatToDo: Rebuild the next run with a curiosity beat between patient-flow story and decision. Let physicians feel the unresolved bottleneck before the software appears.
examples.whyItMatters: The decision failed because it arrived before desire. Intrigue keeps the room mentally active long enough for the rollout to feel like an answer.

examples.title: Marc Puts the Terms Sheet Last

planSpec.domain: boutique hotel owner seeking a construction loan for a fire-damaged inn
planSpec.audience: an owner whose emotional story needs order to become financeable
planSpec.stakes: the lender hears sentimental restoration instead of controlled demand and repayment logic
planSpec.requiredBeat: he lays loan documents in sequence and notices the hookpoint only works after the occupancy rebound story

examples.scenario: Marc sets a charred porch baluster beside his clean loan term sheet on the inn's dining table. He thinks about opening with the fire, then sees the lender hearing sentiment instead of demand. He lays the occupancy graph before the hookpoint and moves the term sheet last, where repayment logic can finally feel earned. The repayment logic can land because Marc lets demand and hookpoint make the term sheet feel earned.
examples.whatToDo: Keep the emotional object, but sequence it after demand and before terms. Let the hookpoint rise from occupancy evidence, not from damage alone.
examples.whyItMatters: The baluster can create feeling, but feeling without order sounds risky to a lender. The sequence turns restoration into a financeable case.

examples.title: Julia Shuts the Robot Case

planSpec.domain: ocean-cleanup robotics team pitching a marina pilot to harbor commissioners
planSpec.audience: engineers who tend to demo the machine before defining the room's frame
planSpec.stakes: commissioners dismiss the robot as a gadget before seeing the debris cost
planSpec.requiredBeat: the team lead shuts the demo case and starts instead with who controls the marina's reputation after holiday trash weekends

examples.scenario: Julia keeps a sealed robot case beside a bucket of tangled fishing line and the holiday trash log. Her engineers are ready to open the case for the harbor commissioners. Her hand rests on the latch. She must decide whether to demo first or shut the case and start with who owns the marina's reputation after trash weekends. The closed case keeps the commissioners inside the reputation frame before the robot becomes the answer.
examples.whatToDo: Shut the case and set the frame around reputation and cleanup cost. Let the robot enter later as the answer to a problem the commissioners already accept.
examples.whyItMatters: A demo without frame looks like a gadget. Sequence makes the machine useful because the room first understands the decision it is making.

examples.title: Sofia Moves the Terms Sheet

planSpec.domain: university licensing officer pitching a battery patent to a materials manufacturer
planSpec.audience: a licensing officer who has the data but no live sequence
planSpec.stakes: the manufacturer files the patent as speculative unless intrigue and prize build before terms
planSpec.requiredBeat: she asks the room to imagine the competitor signing first, then moves the terms sheet to the end of the packet

examples.scenario: Sofia holds her licensing packet in a manufacturer's materials lab: a patent diagram clipped to a graphite sample pouch, with the terms sheet on top. If the room sees terms first, the battery patent sounds speculative. Sofia must decide whether to ask them to picture a competitor signing first, then move terms to the end where prize and decision belong. The shifted packet prevents Sofia from asking for terms before the manufacturer feels prize and decision pressure.
examples.whatToDo: Build sequence before terms. Frame the opportunity, tell the competitive story, raise intrigue around timing, then let terms arrive after value feels selective.
examples.whyItMatters: Terms at the front make the patent a transaction. Terms after intrigue and prize make the same patent feel like access to a scarce advantage.

questions.prompt: A pitch team has strong frame, story, intrigue, prize, hookpoint, and decision notes, but they plan to present them in whatever order feels natural. What is the main risk?
choices: The pieces may arrive before the room is ready to receive them.
The room may notice the acronym too quickly.
The pitch may sound too brief.
questions.explanation: STRONG is an order of handoffs. A strong piece can weaken if it arrives before the prior move has prepared the room.

questions.prompt: A port developer wants to open with megawatt output in a lease vote. The room is politically tense. Which first move fits the method? The listener has not rejected the idea; the room is simply meeting the steps in the wrong order.
choices: Show the turbine efficiency chart first.
Set the frame around what kind of lease decision the port is making.
Ask for the lease vote before details distract the room.
questions.explanation: Frame comes before output because it shapes how the output will be judged. Asking early pressures the room, and an efficiency chart can be misread inside the wrong frame.

questions.prompt: A hospital workflow pitch tells the patient-flow story and immediately asks for pilot approval. Physicians resist. Which missing move should the team inspect?
choices: Prize, because the room needs scarcity before any story.
Frame, because pilots never trust software.
Intrigue, because the team jumped from story to decision before curiosity was alive.
questions.explanation: The gap is the missing curiosity handoff. The room heard stakes but did not yet feel the unresolved tension that would make the pilot welcome.

questions.prompt: A sponsorship director opens with attendance numbers and the bank treats the package as logo inventory. What sequence correction is strongest? The sequence is visible on the table, and one misplaced beat would make the room judge the offer too early.
choices: Move community story and status before attendance and access.
Remove attendance numbers because numbers make offers generic.
Start with the contract terms to show seriousness.
questions.explanation: Community story changes what the numbers mean. Removing numbers wastes proof, and terms too early turn the package into procurement.

questions.prompt: An inn owner has a powerful fire-damage object and a clean loan sheet. Why should the occupancy rebound story come before the loan terms? The listener has not rejected the idea; the room is simply meeting the steps in the wrong order.
choices: Because lenders prefer emotional openings.
Because repayment logic needs demand evidence before terms are judged.
Because the terms should be hidden until the end.
questions.explanation: The rebound story makes the loan financeable. The object creates attention, but demand evidence lets terms feel controlled rather than sentimental.

questions.prompt: A robotics team wants to open a demo case before marina commissioners understand holiday cleanup costs. What is the likely failure? The team has only a few minutes, so compression has to preserve the handoffs rather than erase them.
choices: The robot will look too technically advanced.
The commissioners will ask for a longer demo.
The robot will be judged as a gadget instead of an answer.
questions.explanation: Without frame and story, the demo has no decision context. The same robot lands better after reputation and cleanup cost are clear.

questions.prompt: A licensing officer puts patent terms first and the manufacturer calls the technology speculative. What should she change? The sequence is visible on the table, and one misplaced beat would make the room judge the offer too early.
choices: Build frame, intrigue, and prize before terms.
Add more legal detail to the first page.
Delay all mention of competitors until after signing.
questions.explanation: Terms need perceived value before they can land. More legal detail repeats the transactional frame, while competitor timing can create useful intrigue.

questions.prompt: A manager says STRONG should be followed word for word in every room. Which evaluation is best? The listener has not rejected the idea; the room is simply meeting the steps in the wrong order.
choices: Correct, because scripts prevent improvising.
Too rigid, because the sequence guides handoffs while pacing still requires judgment.
Incorrect only when the pitch is longer than ten minutes.
questions.explanation: The method is a route, not a fixed transcript. Length and pacing change, but the handoffs still protect the pitch from scattering.

questions.prompt: During a ten-minute partner pitch, the team wants to use its sharpest line before anyone understands the customer story. A team has a sharp hookpoint but no story before it. What problem should they expect?
choices: The hookpoint may sound like a slogan because no sequence earned it.
The decision will become too easy for the room.
The frame will automatically become stronger.
questions.explanation: A peak needs setup. Without story and intrigue, a sharp line has nothing beneath it and can feel like marketing decoration.

reviewCards.front: What does STRONG give you besides a list of moves?
reviewCards.back: It gives you an order of handoffs. Each move prepares the room for the next one, from frame through decision.

reviewCards.front: A hookpoint feels clever but hollow. Which earlier moves may be missing?
reviewCards.back: Check story and intrigue. A hookpoint needs a sequence behind it or it becomes a slogan instead of a peak.

reviewCards.front: Why is decision last in the sequence?
reviewCards.back: The room needs value, desire, and fit before an ask feels clean. A decision too early often reads as pressure.

reviewCards.front: A demo is impressive but the room shrugs. What sequence issue should you inspect?
reviewCards.back: The demo may have appeared before frame and story. Define the decision and stakes first so the demo becomes an answer.

reviewCards.front: How should you use STRONG under time pressure?
reviewCards.back: Compress the beats, but keep the handoffs. Do not let pressure make you dump every fact or skip straight to the ask.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to treat STRONG as a live route through the room. The skill is knowing which move should come next when pressure tempts you to skip ahead.

ifThenPlans.plan: If your outline starts with proof, then ask what frame the room needs before that proof appears.
If you want to show the product first, then write the decision the demo is supposed to answer before opening the case.
If terms appear early, then move them after story, intrigue, and prize unless the room has already earned that stage.
If one beat takes more than a third of your time, then cut it until the next handoff can happen clearly.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Take one pitch and make six index-card lines for STRONG. Move any proof, terms, or ask that appears before its setup.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For every pitch this week, note which STRONG move felt rushed. Rewrite that handoff before the next room, not the whole pitch.

memorableLines.text: The order teaches the room what to feel next.
memorableLines.why: It states the distinction between a method and a mnemonic.

memorableLines.text: The same material now has a spine.
memorableLines.why: It makes sequence feel concrete without overexplaining it.

memorableLines.text: A pitch with the right pieces in the wrong order still loses force.
memorableLines.why: It captures the danger of treating STRONG as interchangeable tips.
